material_requests.title: Procurement 3 — Material Requests: Demand Made Visible
material_requests.desc: Material Requests and the demand machinery in ZhiftERP: the field walk — type routing, need dates, justifications, and the status life; the three demand sources — manual requests, reorder auto-generation on projected quantity with the computation as justification, and order-driven demand; the screening step — stock elsewhere first, the need as stated, size and date, budget and policy — with the approval-band separation and the purchases-avoided figure; consolidation — the worksheet, the ordering arithmetic with written adjustments, the date and destination structures, the request-to-order trace, and the window discipline; transfer and issue requests with the cascade rule from branch demand to hub purchasing; and the five demand reads including the quarterly trace audit.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The Material Request: scope and position
lessons.html:
This module covers the Material Request and the demand machinery in ZhiftERP. On completing this module you will be able to: complete the Material Request field walk; state the four request types and what each routes to; operate the three demand sources including reorder auto-generation; run the screening step that stands between demand and commitment; consolidate requests into purchase demand with the ordering arithmetic; handle transfer and issue requests at the module boundary; and run the demand reads.

What a Material Request is. The Material Request is the demand document: a recorded statement that some part of the business needs some quantity of some item by some date. It commits nothing — no stock moves, no money is promised, no supplier is engaged. Its function is to make demand explicit, attributable, and reviewable before anything is committed, which is the structural difference between a purchasing function that responds to recorded demand and one that responds to corridor conversations.

Position in the flow. Demand precedes commitment: the Material Request sits before the Request for Quotation and the Purchase Order (modules 4-5), and before the transfer machinery on the internal side. The sequence — need recorded, need screened, need consolidated, then committed — gives the buying decision its shape: the Purchase Order commits against screened, consolidated demand, and every order line traces back to the requests that justified it.

The four types. The Material Request Type field routes the demand:

1. Purchase — the demand becomes buying: the type this track's modules 4-5 consume.
2. Material Transfer — the demand is met from another warehouse: the branch replenishment lane the Inventory track's module 6 operates.
3. Material Issue — the demand is internal consumption: stock issued to a department or purpose through the issue lane.
4. Manufacture — the demand routes to production, where the site runs the manufacturing lane.

The type is a routing decision made at the request, and Chapter 6 covers the boundary cases — including the transfer request that becomes purchase demand when the network cannot cover it.

Custody. Requests are raised by the roles the matrix permits (branch supervisors, department heads, and the reorder machinery itself); screening is the procurement function's step; approval bands per the matrix; and the standing rule: demand is recorded before it is met — no order without its requests, no request without its stated need.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the field walk. Chapter 3: demand sources. Chapter 4: screening. Chapter 5: consolidation. Chapter 6: transfers and issues. Chapter 7: the demand reads. Chapter 8: worked example. Chapter 9: review and the module rule.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Material Request doctype
lessons.html:
Open Material Request (awesome bar) > New. Complete the fields in order.

1. Material Request Type. The routing decision (Chapter 1): Purchase, Material Transfer, Material Issue, or Manufacture. The type determines which machinery consumes the request and what the warehouse fields mean, so it is set first and set correctly — a transfer need typed as a purchase generates buying for stock the network already holds.

2. Requested By and the requesting context. Who raises the request, and for which part of the business — the branch, department, or cost centre per the site's fields. Attribution matters operationally: the demand reads (Chapter 7) aggregate by requester, and the screening step (Chapter 4) evaluates need in the requester's context.

3. Required By Date. The date the need becomes real — when the branch runs out, when the job starts, when the stock is needed on the shelf. The honest-date rule applies in a specific form here: the required-by date is the need date, not the wish date. Dates padded early teach the system's readers to discount them; dates entered late guarantee expediting. Every downstream schedule — the quotation cycle, the order's delivery date, the import consignment calendar — computes backward from this field.

4. The items table. Per row:

1. Item and quantity in the stated unit — the unit column read per the standing discipline; branch requests in cartons and counts in units are the module 2 pairing rule's territory.
2. The warehouse fields per type — for Purchase: the warehouse the goods should arrive into; for Material Transfer: the source and target of the movement; for Material Issue: the warehouse issuing. The fields state where the need physically is.
3. The per-row required-by date where needs differ by line.

5. The justification. The stated need — the reorder computation for auto-generated requests (Chapter 3), the branch's sales cover statement, the department's purpose for an issue. One line suffices; its presence is what the screening step reads, and a request whose need cannot be stated in a line is a request the screen returns to its raiser.

6. Save, submit, and the status life. Submission enters the request into the demand pipeline. The status tracks its life: Pending, Partially Ordered, Ordered (for purchase types — the %ordered figure per row), Transferred or Issued for the internal types, and Stopped for demand deliberately ended (Chapter 7's hygiene). A request is never deleted to make it go away; it is stopped with its reason, so the demand record stays complete.

Verification per request. The type correct for the need; the requester and context attributed; the date the need date; quantities in read units against stated warehouses; the justification present.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Demand sources
lessons.html:
Demand enters the pipeline from three sources. This chapter is each source and its rules.

1. Manual requests. Branches and departments raise requests for what they need: the branch's stock request ahead of a promotion, the department's consumables, the clinic's equipment need. The rules:

1. Raised by the permitted roles in the requester's own context — the branch requests for the branch.
2. Justified in a line (Chapter 2.5) — the sales cover, the purpose, the event.
3. Dated honestly — the need date, computed from the requester's own arithmetic (the branch that sells forty units a week and holds eighty knows its date).

2. Reorder auto-generation. The Inventory track's module 6 machinery: reorder levels on the item-warehouse rows, evaluated against projected quantity — actual stock minus reservations plus incoming orders — so the computation sees commitments in both directions. When projected quantity falls below the reorder level, the system generates a Material Request for the reorder quantity:

1. The generated request carries its computation as its justification — the level, the projected figure, the shortfall: screened like any other demand, not treated as pre-approved because a machine raised it.
2. The parameters are module 2's planning fields — measured lead times, costed safety stock, quantities in carton multiples: the auto-trigger is only as good as the fields it computes from, and the planning review is where its quality is maintained.
3. The generation runs on the configured schedule, and the reorder review (the weekly pass the Inventory track defined) reads what it generated before the screen consumes it.

3. Order-driven demand. Sales commitments generate purchase demand where stock will not cover them: the enterprise order whose equipment must be bought (the Selling track's BizRetail Ltd case triggered exactly this), the made-to-order line, the special. The rules: the demand references its driving order, its date computes backward from the order's delivery schedule with the lead time (module 2's field), and its quantities are the order's quantities — demand that borrows an order's justification to buy extra is padding the screen exists to catch.

4. The source mix as information. The demand pattern read (Chapter 7) splits the pipeline by source. The mix is operationally meaningful: a network whose demand is mostly auto-generated runs on its parameters (and its exceptions are parameter questions); one whose demand is mostly manual runs on judgment (and its exceptions are screening questions); order-driven spikes are the commercial calendar showing through. The read states the mix; the review acts on what it states.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — The screening step
lessons.html:
Between recorded demand and committed money stands one procedure. This chapter is the screen.

1. What screening is. The procurement function's review of submitted requests before they consolidate into buying: each request confirmed as a genuine, correctly-sized, correctly-dated need that the network cannot meet more cheaply from what it already holds. Screening runs on the demand pipeline's cadence (daily or per the volume), and its output is requests passed, returned, or resized — each with its note.

2. The screening checks, in order.

1. Stock elsewhere first. Before any purchase: does the network hold this item idle somewhere? The Inventory track's rebalancing lane (module 7) is the first answer to demand — the lateral transfer from a branch holding dead stock costs transport; the purchase costs the full landed figure. The screen queries network stock as its first act, and a purchase request for an item another warehouse holds in excess converts to a transfer request with the note.
2. The need as stated. The justification against the requester's context: the branch's sales cover arithmetic sampled against its actual sell-through (the reads the Inventory track's module 6 built serve here); the department's purpose against its pattern. Returned requests state what was missing.
3. The size and the date. Quantity against the stated need (the pairing rule catching unit errors — a branch requesting 15 when it means 15 cartons, or the reverse); the date against the real calendar.
4. Budget and policy where configured — the request against its cost centre's frame, per the site's budget configuration; policy items (restricted classes, approval-required categories) routed to their named approvers.

3. Approval bands. Screened demand approves per the matrix: routine replenishment within the standing bands; above-band or exceptional demand to the named approvers with the screen's notes attached. The approval attaches to the demand before the money is committed — module 5's Purchase Order approval then reviews the commitment (supplier, price, terms), not the need, because the need was settled here. The two approvals ask different questions, and keeping them separate is what keeps both short.

4. The screen's record. Each screening pass files its list: requests passed with sizes confirmed, returned with reasons, converted to transfers with the stock they found. The monthly screening read (Chapter 7) samples the passes — and the specific figure it tracks is stated plainly: purchases avoided by the stock-elsewhere check, in naira, because that figure is the screen's measurable contribution and the reason the step exists.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Consolidation
lessons.html:
Screened demand consolidates into buying. This chapter is the worksheet and the arithmetic.

1. Why consolidation. The same item is demanded from several sources in the same window — the hub's reorder trigger, two branches' requests. Ordering each separately produces three small orders, three deliveries, three receipts, and none of the volume terms the supplier's price breaks offer. Consolidation combines the demand into one purchase decision per item per supplier per window, and the trace (below) keeps every source visible inside it.

2. The consolidation worksheet. Per buying window, per item:

1. The demand lines — each open, screened request row for the item: source, quantity, required-by date, destination warehouse.
2. The consolidated quantity — the sum, adjusted by the ordering arithmetic below.
3. The date structure — the earliest genuine need date governs the order's first delivery; where sources need at different dates, the consolidated order carries the schedule (module 5's per-row dates and split deliveries serve exactly this).
4. The destination structure — where the goods should land: the hub for onward distribution in the standing network pattern, or split destinations where the supplier delivers direct per the arrangement.

3. The ordering arithmetic. The consolidated quantity is shaped by module 2's constraints, applied in order: the purchase unit's multiples (orders in whole cartons), the supplier's minimums, the price-break thresholds where crossing one is priced against carrying the extra (the module 4 quotations state the breaks; the worksheet shows the comparison), and the import consignment arithmetic on foreign lines. Each adjustment above the raw demand is written on the worksheet with its reason — the excess is a decided figure, not a rounding accident.

4. The request-to-order trace. The Purchase Order (module 5) creates against the consolidated demand, and the system links each order row to its requests: %ordered advances on every source request as the order commits. The trace answers, in both directions, the two standing questions: which requests does this order serve (the order's justification), and where is my request (the requester's status view). A consolidation that loses its trace turns the demand pipeline into a suggestion box; the linkage is maintained as part of creating the order, not reconstructed afterward.

5. The window discipline. Consolidation runs on the buying calendar — the weekly window for domestic replenishment, the consignment calendar for imports — and demand arriving after a window closes waits for the next unless its date cannot wait, in which case it is the expedite lane with its named approval and its premium visible. The calendar is what makes consolidation possible; a pipeline ordered continuously in dribbles consolidates nothing.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Transfer and issue requests
lessons.html:
Two request types stay internal. This chapter is their handling and the boundary where internal demand becomes buying.

1. Material Transfer requests. The branch replenishment lane: the branch (or the reorder machinery evaluating the branch's rows) requests stock from the hub. The mechanics belong to the Inventory track's module 6 — the weekly replenishment run, the two-step transfer with the transit warehouse, the receiving confirmation — and this module's contribution is the demand side: the request raised, dated, and justified per Chapter 2, consumed by the transfer run.

2. The cascade: when transfer demand becomes purchase demand. The standing network pattern is hub-and-spoke: branches request from the hub; the hub buys from suppliers. The cascade rule:

1. The branch's request is always a transfer request — the branch's relationship is with the hub, and branch-level purchasing is the exception lane the network policy defines (the Inventory track's exception purchase lane), not a routing choice.
2. The hub's coverage check — the transfer run evaluates the hub's projected stock against the requested transfers: covered demand transfers on the run's schedule.
3. Uncovered demand cascades — the shortfall becomes purchase demand at the hub: the hub's reorder row may already have triggered (the projected figure fell as the transfer reservations landed), or the screen raises the purchase demand explicitly with the branch requests as its justification. Either way the consolidation worksheet (Chapter 5) shows the branch demand inside the purchase quantity, and the trace runs branch request → hub purchase → order.

3. Material Issue requests. Internal consumption — consumables to a department, materials to a project — requested, screened for purpose, and issued through the Inventory issue lane with the cost landing on the consuming context per the accountant's design. The issue request's discipline is the purpose statement: issues aggregate into the consumption reads, and unattributed consumption is the leak those reads exist to find.

4. The boundary, stated. This module owns demand and its screening; the Inventory track owns the movement machinery (transfers, issues, the transit discipline); modules 4-5 own the buying that uncovered demand becomes. The documents keep the boundary visible: the request states the need, the transfer or issue documents the internal movement, the order documents the commitment — one need, each stage on its own record, the trace connecting them.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The demand reads
lessons.html:
The standing reads on the demand pipeline, each with its cadence and action.

1. The open-demand read — weekly. All open requests by age, status, and required-by date:

1. Approaching dates — open requests whose need dates fall inside the buying lead time: each is either in a consolidation window, on an order (%ordered advancing), or a problem named now while expediting is still an option.
2. The aging tail — requests open past the policy's window with no ordering activity: each chased to its state — superseded (stopped with reason), waiting on a window (noted), or lost in the pipeline (the process finding).

2. The %ordered read — weekly, with the open-demand pass. Partially ordered requests: the unordered remainder confirmed as still needed (demand shrinks as reality changes — the remainder is re-screened, not automatically carried) or stopped. The figure per request is the requester's answer to where is my request, and keeping it true is what makes the pipeline trustworthy to its users.

3. The stale and stopped hygiene — monthly. Requests stopped in the month with their reasons aggregated; open requests with passed dates and no action swept into decisions. The pipeline's target state matches every other register in the programme: only live demand, because the consolidation worksheets and the buying calendar compute from it.

4. The demand pattern read — monthly. The pipeline by source (Chapter 3.4), requester, and item class:

1. The source mix and its movement — auto-generation's share rising as parameters mature is the intended direction; manual spikes trace to their events.
2. The requester patterns — branches whose requests consistently resize at screening (over-asking as negotiation) are a conversation with data; branches that never request until stock-out are the opposite conversation.
3. The screening figures — returned and converted requests by reason, and the purchases-avoided figure (Chapter 4.4) stated in naira.

5. The trace audit — quarterly. A sample of the quarter's Purchase Orders walked backward: each order row to its requests, each request to its justification. The audit confirms the standing rule holds — no order without its demand — and its findings are process corrections: the order raised without requests (the corridor purchase the pipeline exists to end), the trace lost at consolidation, the justification that was a formality. The audit files with the procurement function's quarterly records, alongside the module 8 scorecard cycle.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Worked example: the 300-carton consolidation
lessons.html:
This chapter runs the demand machinery through the standing case: the PARA-500 purchase that module 5 will place with Emzor. Values and outcomes are listed per step.

Step 1 — the auto-trigger (Chapter 3). The weekly reorder evaluation at Central Warehouse computes PARA-500's projected quantity — actual stock minus the sales reservations, plus nothing incoming — below the reorder level. The machinery generates a Material Request, type Purchase, for 260 cartons, carrying its computation as the justification: the level, the projected figure, the shortfall, the reorder quantity in carton multiples per the planning fields.

Step 2 — the branch requests (Chapters 3, 6). The same week, two branches raise transfer requests for PARA-500 ahead of their local demand: Ibadan for 15 cartons, Akure for 25 cartons — each justified with its sales cover arithmetic, each dated to its need. The transfer run's coverage check finds the hub's projected stock — already below reorder — cannot cover the transfers: the branch demand cascades into the hub's purchase demand per the cascade rule, the branch requests standing as part of its justification.

Step 3 — the screen (Chapter 4). The screening pass works the three demands: the stock-elsewhere check runs first and finds no idle PARA-500 anywhere in the network (the rebalancing lane has nothing to offer — this is genuine new demand); the branch arithmetic samples clean against sell-through; the units read correctly (cartons throughout, per the pairing rule); the dates hold. All three pass, with the screen's notes filed.

Step 4 — the consolidation worksheet (Chapter 5). The buying window consolidates PARA-500: 260 (Central reorder) + 15 (Ibadan) + 25 (Akure) = 300 cartons. The ordering arithmetic confirms the figure: whole cartons already; above Emzor's minimum; the quantity sits at the volume band the standing arrangement prices (module 4's cycle established the rates — the order will place at ₦9,600 per carton). The date structure records the earliest genuine need — Central's cover date — and notes that the branches' dates allow the second drop: the worksheet anticipates the two-drop schedule module 5 will commit (180 next week, 120 the week after), driven by the dates the requests stated.

Step 5 — the trace stands (Chapters 5, 7). Module 5's Purchase Order will create against this consolidated demand, and at that moment %ordered advances on all three requests: the Central trigger, Ibadan's 15, Akure's 25 — each requester's status view answering where their request went. The quarter's trace audit will walk this order backward and find the complete chain: order → worksheet → three requests → three justifications — the standing rule holding: no order without its demand.

The pipeline evidence. The requests with their justifications; the screen's pass with the stock-elsewhere check recorded; the worksheet with the arithmetic and the date structure; the trace ready for the order. Module 4 covers how the Emzor rates on this worksheet were established; module 5 places the commitment.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common errors and the module rule
lessons.html:
The errors that recur in demand management, each with its correction and prevention.

Error 1 — the corridor purchase. Symptom: Purchase Orders raised from conversations with no requests behind them; demand invisible, unattributable, unscreened. Correction: the demand recorded retroactively where the purchase was genuine; the trace audit's finding filed. Prevention: the standing rule enforced in configuration where the site gates orders on requests, and the quarterly trace audit.

Error 2 — the wish date. Symptom: required-by dates padded early as negotiation or entered late as afterthought; downstream schedules computing from fiction; readers discounting all dates. Correction: dates corrected to need dates at screening. Prevention: the need-date rule and the screening date check.

Error 3 — the purchase for stock the network holds. Symptom: buying while another warehouse holds the item in excess; dead stock accumulating at one site while money is spent at another. Correction: the request converted to a transfer; the purchase avoided. Prevention: the stock-elsewhere check as the screen's first act, with its avoided-purchases figure read monthly.

Error 4 — auto-generation treated as pre-approved. Symptom: machine-generated requests ordered without screening; parameter errors (a stale reorder level, an optimistic lead time) buying at scale. Correction: the parameters reviewed; the excess handled through the stock-health lanes. Prevention: generated requests screened like any other, and the planning review maintaining the fields.

Error 5 — the lost trace. Symptom: orders that cannot name their requests; requesters who cannot find their demand; %ordered figures meaning nothing. Correction: the linkage rebuilt for open documents. Prevention: the trace maintained as part of order creation, and the quarterly audit.

Error 6 — the immortal request. Symptom: open requests aging past their dates and their needs; the pipeline cluttered with dead demand; consolidation worksheets summing fiction. Correction: the aging tail swept — stopped with reasons or re-dated as re-screened demand. Prevention: the weekly open-demand read and the monthly hygiene.

Review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: complete the request walk with the type routing, need dates, and justifications; operate the three demand sources including the auto-trigger's computation; run the four screening checks in order with the approval-band separation; consolidate with the worksheet, the ordering arithmetic, and the window discipline; handle the transfer cascade and the issue lane at the boundary; and run the five demand reads.

Module rule 3: demand is recorded before it is met — typed correctly, dated to the need, justified in a line, screened with stock-elsewhere first, consolidated by the worksheet's written arithmetic, and traced so that every order names its requests and every requester can find their demand. Module 4 covers Requests for Quotation and the comparison cycle.

rfq_quotes.title: Procurement 4 — RFQs & Supplier Quotations: The Sourcing Craft
rfq_quotes.desc: Requests for Quotation and the comparison cycle in ZhiftERP: when the policy requires competitive quotes and the named recorded exceptions; the Request for Quotation walk — supplier selection, consolidated quantities, the complete message, and the managed response window; Supplier Quotation entry from attached documents with the pairing rule, tiered breaks, and foreign-currency handling; the comparison worksheet with the landed centre column and the stated criteria; the award decision — best total position, split awards, the decision minute with alternatives, and the updates to lists, orders, and supplier files; negotiation from the recorded position, volume bands, standing arrangements with real validity, and the owned re-quote calendar; and the five cycle reads including the quarterly savings record.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The quotation cycle: scope and position
lessons.html:
This module covers Requests for Quotation, Supplier Quotations, and the comparison cycle in ZhiftERP. On completing this module you will be able to: state when the policy requires competitive quotation; complete the Request for Quotation walk and issue it to suppliers; enter Supplier Quotations from source documents; build the comparison worksheet with landed figures; run the award decision with its criteria and record; conduct the negotiation round and establish standing arrangements; and run the cycle reads.

What the cycle is. The quotation cycle converts screened demand into priced supply options and a recorded award decision: the business asks named suppliers what they would charge, records what each answered, compares the answers on stated criteria, and decides — with the decision, its reasoning, and its alternatives filed. The cycle's product is not only a price: it is the negotiation memory module 2's buying lists draw their sourced rates from, and the record every later price conversation is conducted against.

When the cycle is required. Per the written procurement policy:

1. By value — purchases above the policy's threshold require competitive quotes (the number of quotes per band stated in the policy).
2. By class — the classes the policy names (new items, capital equipment, annual arrangements) quote regardless of single-purchase value, because the arrangement's total exposure is the relevant figure.
3. The exceptions, named — single-source items (the sole manufacturer of a registered product), genuine emergencies through the expedite lane, and repeat purchases inside a standing arrangement's validity — each exception recorded with its reason, because an unrecorded exception is indistinguishable from an avoided control.

Position in the flow. Demand (module 3) precedes the cycle; the cycle's award feeds the Purchase Order (module 5) and the buying lists (module 2); the supplier's later performance (module 8's scorecards) feeds the next cycle's comparison. The sequence gives procurement its accountability shape: every rate on an order traces to a quotation or arrangement, and every award can state why it was made.

Custody. The procurement function runs the cycle; award decisions approve per the matrix's bands; the comparison and decision records file per the one-lookup standard; and the standing rule: a quoted rate is evidence — entered from the supplier's document, compared landed, awarded by stated criteria, and filed with its alternatives.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the Request for Quotation. Chapter 3: Supplier Quotation entry. Chapter 4: the comparison worksheet. Chapter 5: the award decision. Chapter 6: negotiation and arrangements. Chapter 7: the cycle reads. Chapter 8: worked example. Chapter 9: review and the module rule.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Request for Quotation
lessons.html:
Open Request for Quotation (awesome bar) > New. Complete the fields in order.

1. The suppliers table. The named suppliers the request goes to — selected from the register (module 1's gate is the entry point; the cycle does not quote unregistered parties), per the policy's count for the band, drawn from the classes the item belongs to. Supplier selection is itself recorded reasoning: the incumbents, the qualified alternatives, and — where the read shows the same short list every cycle — the deliberate widening the competitiveness review directs.

2. The items table. Drawn from the driving Material Requests (the link carries the demand trace through the cycle):

1. Item, quantity, and unit — the consolidated quantities from module 3's worksheet, in the purchase units, because rates will be quoted against these quantities and volume terms depend on them.
2. Required-by schedule — the dates the demand stated: suppliers quote lead times against real dates.
3. Warehouse — the delivery destination, because delivered-to-where is part of what is being priced (the supplier's included delivery versus ex-works collection changes the landed comparison).

3. The message to suppliers. The request's terms: the response deadline, the validity period expected on quotes, the requirement to state price breaks, minimums, lead times, and payment terms, and the specification references for items that carry them. A request that does not ask for breaks and terms receives quotes that omit them, and the comparison then runs on incomplete columns — the request's completeness determines the comparison's.

4. Issuing the request. The request sends per the site's channels — the emailed document, or the supplier portal link where the site operates portal quoting (suppliers entering their own rates against the request, which lands the responses as draft Supplier Quotations directly). Either channel, the same record rule: what was asked, of whom, by when, filed on the request.

5. The response window. The deadline is managed, not hoped: the reminder at the mid-point to non-responders, the response log as quotes arrive, and the close at the deadline — late quotes admitted only by the recorded exception (the policy states when), because a comparison whose window silently extends for one supplier is not the level comparison the file claims. Non-response is itself data: the response-rate read (Chapter 7) accumulates it per supplier, and module 8's relationship review consumes it.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Supplier Quotation entry
lessons.html:
Each response is recorded as a Supplier Quotation. This chapter is the entry discipline.

1. The Supplier Quotation doctype. Open Supplier Quotation (awesome bar) — or receive it from the portal as a draft. The record per responding supplier:

1. The supplier and the request reference — the link to the Request for Quotation carrying the cycle's thread.
2. The items table — the quoted rate per item per unit, the quoted lead time, and the quantity terms.
3. Validity — the date the quote holds until: the field the award clock runs against, and the field the re-quote cadence (Chapter 6) watches.
4. Terms — payment terms offered, delivery terms (included delivery or ex-works — the landed comparison's input), and any conditions the supplier attaches.

2. The entry discipline. Quotes entered by the procurement function follow the evidence rule:

1. From the supplier's document — the emailed quotation, the price circular, the signed offer — attached to the Supplier Quotation. The record states what the supplier stated; the attachment proves it. A rate entered from a phone call is entered with the call noted and confirmed in writing before the comparison closes, because an award justified by an unverifiable rate is an award that cannot defend itself.
2. The pairing rule at entry — the quoted rate belongs to a quoted unit: ₦9,600 per Carton-12 entered as such, never transcribed onto a unit line. Transcription is where comparison errors are born, and the entry check reads quantity-unit-rate together per the standing discipline.
3. Breaks entered as breaks — a supplier quoting tiered rates (one rate to 199 cartons, a better rate from 200, better again from 300) has each tier recorded, because the comparison at the consolidated quantity needs the tier that quantity lands in, and the consolidation arithmetic (module 3) may deliberately cross a tier.

3. Foreign-currency quotes. The Indian manufacturer quotes in dollars: the Supplier Quotation carries the quoted currency and rate as quoted, and the comparison worksheet (Chapter 4) does the conversion at the planning rate — the quote records the supplier's statement; the worksheet does the arithmetic. Converting at entry buries the exposure the comparison must show.

4. Clarifications. Ambiguities — a quote silent on delivery terms, a break structure unclear — are resolved by written question and answer filed with the quotation, before comparison. A comparison built on assumed readings of ambiguous quotes produces awards the supplier will dispute at the first invoice.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — The comparison worksheet
lessons.html:
Recorded quotes compare on one worksheet. This chapter is its columns and its rules.

1. The worksheet's shape. Per item (or per lot where items award together): one row per quoting supplier, columns per criterion, the consolidated quantity from module 3 as the comparison quantity, and the file reference per row to the Supplier Quotation it summarises. The worksheet is a record, not a scratchpad: it files with the decision, and the trace audit expects to find it.

2. The landed column — the comparison's centre. Per module 2's comparison rule, suppliers compare landed, never ex-works:

1. Domestic quotes with included delivery — the quoted rate is close to the landed figure; the worksheet notes any excluded charges.
2. Ex-works and foreign quotes — the landed worksheet (module 2, Chapter 7) computes the full figure: goods value converted at the planning rate, plus freight, insurance, duties, clearing, and haulage. The Indian manufacturer's attractive dollar rate is compared only after it becomes a naira-per-unit-on-the-shelf figure.
3. The rule in one sentence: the comparison column is what the item will cost on the shelf, from each supplier, at the comparison quantity — anything else compares fragments.

3. The other columns. Price is one criterion:

1. Lead time — quoted, and adjusted by the supplier's measured reality where module 8's data exists (a quoted two weeks from a supplier whose measured performance is four is entered as quoted with the measured figure beside it).
2. Payment terms — the working-capital value of offered terms, computed per the accountant's arithmetic where terms differ materially.
3. Quality and performance — the scorecard figures (module 8) for known suppliers: on-time rate, damage rate, dispute history. New suppliers carry their verification status and any trial-order condition.
4. Minimums, breaks, and validity — stated per quote, with the break tier at the comparison quantity marked.

4. The total-cost view. Where criteria pull in different directions, the worksheet computes the comparable total: the landed rate at the comparison quantity, adjusted for the terms value, with the risk criteria (lead time, performance) stated beside the money rather than converted into it by invented weights. The decision (Chapter 5) weighs the stated figures; the worksheet's job is to state them honestly and completely, one page per item, readable by an approver who was not in the cycle.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — The award decision
lessons.html:
The comparison feeds a decision. This chapter is the criteria, the record, and what the award updates.

1. The decision criteria. Per the written policy, the award goes to the best total position, not reflexively to the lowest rate:

1. The landed figure at the real quantity — the money criterion, from the worksheet's centre column.
2. Supply reliability — the measured performance and lead time against the demand's dates: the lowest rate that arrives late costs its saving in stock-outs, and the policy states how reliability is weighed for the class (essential lines weigh it heavily; discretionary lines less).
3. Terms and relationship structure — the payment terms' value, the arrangement potential (Chapter 6), and the concentration position (module 1's read: an award that deepens a named dependency is made knowingly or not at all).

2. Split awards. The decision may split: the volume line to the best landed position, a secondary share to the qualified alternative — the deliberate dual-sourcing the concentration review recommends on critical classes, priced as the policy allows (the secondary share may carry a premium, stated in the minute as the cost of supply security). A split is a decision with its reasoning, not an inability to decide.

3. The decision minute. One page, filed with the worksheet:

1. The award: supplier(s), items, rates, quantities or bands, terms, validity.
2. The reasoning: the criteria as weighed for this decision, in two or three sentences.
3. The alternatives: what the unsuccessful quotes offered, in one line each — the record that makes next cycle's negotiation informed and this cycle's decision defensible.
4. The approval: per the matrix's band for the award's value.

4. What the award updates.

1. The buying lists — the awarded rates load by the governed update with the minute as their source: module 2's sourced-rates rule closing its loop.
2. The demand pipeline — module 5's Purchase Order creates against the screened demand at the awarded rates; the trace runs request → worksheet → award → order.
3. The supplier file — the award, and equally the non-award, files per supplier: module 8's relationship review reads both.

5. Unsuccessful suppliers. Informed per the policy's courtesy standard — the relationship the business may need next cycle is maintained by the professionalism of this one. The notification's content follows the policy (the fact of the award; commercial details per the confidentiality rules), and the response-rate read expects continued participation as its measure of whether the cycle treats its participants well.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Negotiation and standing arrangements
lessons.html:
The comparison creates a negotiating position; repeat lines convert awards into arrangements. This chapter is both.

1. The negotiation round. Between comparison and award, the policy permits a negotiation round with the leading suppliers:

1. Conducted from the worksheet — the position is the recorded alternatives; the asks are specific (the rate at the volume tier, the terms, the included delivery) and minuted as asked and answered.
2. The level-field rule — the round's structure follows the policy (best-and-final from the shortlist, or sequential negotiation as the policy allows); one supplier's quote is not disclosed to another, because a cycle that leaks quotes teaches suppliers to quote high and wait.
3. The outcome enters the record — negotiated improvements amend the Supplier Quotation (the supplier's confirming document attached) and the worksheet re-states before the award minute writes.

2. Volume bands. The negotiation's standing instrument for repeat lines: the rate agreed per quantity band — the tier structure entered from Chapter 3 becoming the agreed schedule. The consolidated ordering (module 3) then prices predictably: the 300-carton window lands in its band at its rate, and the ordering arithmetic can deliberately reach a band where the worksheet shows the crossing pays.

3. Standing arrangements. For lines bought repeatedly, the award converts into an arrangement — the agreed rates (or bands), terms, and validity period, recorded per the site's instrument (the supplier-specific price structure, or the buying-side blanket order where quantities commit):

1. Inside validity, purchases execute without re-quoting — the module 1 exception operating as designed: the cycle ran once at the arrangement's scale.
2. The validity is real — expiry triggers the re-quote cadence (below); rates do not drift past their period by inattention, per the same rule as the selling side's blanket orders.
3. Price-change requests inside validity — the supplier's increase letter routes to the review: accepted changes are dated amendments with the notice filed; the trend read (module 2) shows what moved and when.

4. The re-quote cadence. Per class in the policy: annual for stable domestic lines, semi-annual where markets move, per-consignment elements on import lines (freight re-quotes with the market even where goods rates hold). The cadence is calendared with the quarterly cycle reads, so re-quoting is scheduled work rather than a response to a supplier's letter — the business that only re-quotes when a supplier raises prices has ceded the calendar to its suppliers.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The cycle reads
lessons.html:
The standing reads on the quotation cycle, each with its cadence and action.

1. The open-cycle read — weekly. Open Requests for Quotation by response deadline and age: reminders to non-responders at the midpoint; cycles past deadline closed and compared; cycles stalled before award chased to their blocking step — a demand pipeline waiting on a stalled cycle is a stock-out forming upstream, and the read connects the two dates.

2. The validity read — weekly. Supplier Quotations and arrangements by days-to-expiry: awards pending against expiring quotes decided before the clock runs out (an award made against an expired quote is a re-quote conducted involuntarily); arrangements approaching expiry entering the re-quote calendar per Chapter 6.

3. The response-rate read — quarterly. Per supplier: requests sent, responses received, response timeliness. The patterns route: the reliable responder is the relationship working; the chronic non-responder is a module 8 conversation (and, unresolved, a register question — a supplier that will not quote is a supplier in name); a class where response rates fall across suppliers is a market signal the review reads.

4. The award pattern read — quarterly. The quarter's awards by supplier, class, and value:

1. The competitiveness figure — cycles with the policy's quote count achieved, against cycles that ran short (with reasons: genuine single-source, or a supplier base too thin — the widening action).
2. The concentration movement — awards' effect on the module 1 concentration figures, read together with the risk review.
3. The incumbency pattern — the incumbent's win rate: a rate near one hundred percent with prices drifting upward is the signal that the cycle has become a formality, and the deliberate-widening action (new qualified suppliers into the next cycle) is its correction.

5. The savings record — quarterly. The cycle's measured contribution: negotiated improvements against first quotes, band crossings that paid, and the avoided-cost figures where re-quoting moved an incumbent's drift back — stated in naira with the cycles referenced, filed with the procurement function's quarterly records alongside module 3's purchases-avoided figure. The two figures together are the demand-and-sourcing machinery's stated value, in money, per quarter — the record the owner's review reads when the function's cost is weighed against its contribution.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Worked example: establishing the Emzor arrangement
lessons.html:
This chapter runs the cycle that produced the ₦9,600 rate the module 3 consolidation priced from. Values and outcomes are listed per step.

The trigger. PARA-500's volume and the class policy (annual arrangements for core pharmaceutical lines) put the line into the annual quotation cycle: the consolidated annual volume justifies arrangement-scale negotiation rather than order-by-order pricing.

Step 1 — the request issues (Chapter 2). The Request for Quotation goes to three registered suppliers: Emzor, the second domestic manufacturer, and the importer channel as the qualified alternative. The items table carries the annual volume structure and the delivery destination (Central Warehouse); the message asks for price breaks by quantity band, payment terms, lead times, and validity; the deadline is set with the mid-point reminder calendared.

Step 2 — the quotations enter (Chapter 3). All three respond. Each Supplier Quotation enters from the supplier's attached document, rates paired to units (per Carton-12 throughout), break structures recorded as tiers — including Emzor's tiering with its band at the 300-carton volume level. The importer's quote notes ex-works terms; the clarification round confirms it in writing.

Step 3 — the comparison (Chapter 4). The worksheet compares landed at the annual and per-window quantities: the domestic manufacturers' included-delivery rates stand nearly as quoted; the importer's rate gains the acquisition layer and loses its apparent advantage — the landed column re-ordering the ranking the raw rates suggested. The other columns fill: lead times (with measured history beside Emzor's quote), terms offered, and the scorecard figures for the incumbents.

Step 4 — negotiation and award (Chapters 5-6). The negotiation round runs from the worksheet with the two domestic manufacturers: the specific asks — the band rate and terms — minuted as asked and answered. The award decision: Emzor takes the volume line at ₦9,600 per Carton-12 at the volume band, on 30-day terms, with the second manufacturer holding a secondary share on the overlap range — the split stated in the minute as the concentration mitigation the module 1 risk review recommended, with its premium visible. The decision minute files with the worksheet: award, reasoning in three sentences, alternatives in a line each, approval per the band.

Step 5 — the award updates the machinery (Chapters 5-6). The rates load onto the buying list by the governed update, the minute as source; the arrangement records with its validity and the re-quote date calendared; the unsuccessful importer is informed per the courtesy standard and remains a responsive participant in the read. When module 3's consolidation later sums 300 cartons, the worksheet prices from this arrangement without re-quoting — the band rate applying exactly as agreed — and module 5's order will commit it.

The cycle evidence. The request with its message; three quotations with attached documents; the worksheet with its landed centre; the negotiation minutes; the decision minute with alternatives; the sourced rate on the list; the calendar entry for re-quote. The rate every PARA-500 order carries is answerable back to this file in one lookup — the negotiation memory the module exists to build.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common errors and the module rule
lessons.html:
The errors that recur in the quotation cycle, each with its correction and prevention.

Error 1 — the ex-works comparison. Symptom: rankings built on raw quoted rates; the import line awarded on a figure that omits its acquisition layer; the shelf cost discovered after commitment. Correction: the worksheet rebuilt landed; the award reviewed. Prevention: the landed column as the comparison's centre, per the module 2 rule.

Error 2 — the unverifiable rate. Symptom: quotes entered from calls with no confirming document; awards that cannot show what the supplier actually offered; disputes at the first invoice. Correction: written confirmation obtained or the quote excluded. Prevention: entry from attached documents, and phone rates confirmed in writing before comparison closes.

Error 3 — the leaked cycle. Symptom: one supplier's rates disclosed to another; suppliers learning to quote high and wait for the leak; the comparison's integrity gone. Correction: the round's records reviewed; the policy's structure re-imposed. Prevention: the level-field rule, and negotiation conducted from the worksheet's recorded position rather than from disclosures.

Error 4 — the formality cycle. Symptom: the incumbent winning every cycle at drifting prices; requests issued to the same short list; the comparison a ritual before a foregone award. Correction: the deliberate widening — new qualified suppliers into the next cycle. Prevention: the award pattern read's incumbency figure, acted on.

Error 5 — the undocumented award. Symptom: rates on orders with no minute behind them; decisions that cannot state their criteria; the next negotiation starting from nothing. Correction: the record reconstructed where evidence allows. Prevention: the decision minute as the award's required form, and the trace audit expecting it.

Error 6 — the expired arrangement still pricing. Symptom: purchases at arrangement rates past validity; increases accepted without dated amendments; the calendar ceded to supplier letters. Correction: the re-quote run; rates re-established. Prevention: the validity read and the calendared re-quote cadence per class.

Review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: state when the policy requires the cycle and the recorded exceptions; issue a complete request with breaks, terms, and deadlines asked; enter quotations from documents with the pairing rule and tiers; build the worksheet with the landed centre and the stated criteria; run the award with its minute, splits, and updates; conduct the negotiation round and maintain arrangements with real validity; and run the five cycle reads with the savings record.

Module rule 4: a quoted rate is evidence — asked completely, entered from the supplier's document, compared landed at the real quantity, awarded by stated criteria in a filed minute with its alternatives, loaded to the lists with its source, and re-quoted on the calendar the business owns. Module 5 covers the Purchase Order.

purchase_orders.title: Procurement 5 — Purchase Orders: The Commitment
purchase_orders.desc: The commitment document: anatomy and creation discipline, the incoming pipeline and fulfilment ledger, status worklists, Hold and Close with the phantom-incoming sweep, amendments and sourcing integrity, and the supplier-promise craft — acknowledgment, honest dates, expediting, and OTIF.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The Purchase Order, field by field
lessons.html:
Everything before this document was preparation — the supplier vetted, the item priced, the need requested, the source competed. The Purchase Order is where your firm COMMITS: money promised to a named supplier for named goods at named rates by named dates. It is the buy-side twin of Selling 4's Sales Order, and if you commanded that module, this one will feel like meeting the same machine from the other side of the counter. Walk the fields:

  • Supplier — the vetted master (Procurement 1), whose currency, payment terms, buying price list and tax defaults land on the document by the default chain. A PO to a supplier on hold refuses per the hold's type — the lifecycle machinery working at the moment of commitment.
  • Transaction date vs required-by dates — when the commitment was made vs when the goods are owed, header-level and refinable per row for staggered supply: the import line at 50 days, the local line at 3, one order, honest schedule. Receiving plans from these dates (Chapter 7's discipline keeps them honest).
  • The items grid — item, quantity, UOM with its conversion (a 300 Carton-12 row is 3,600 units to the stock ledger — Buying 2's arithmetic at the moment it starts costing real money), the rate fetched from the supplier-scoped agreed price (Procurement 2) or carried from the winning quotation (Procurement 4), and per row the target warehouse — where the goods will be received, inherited from the request and inherited BY the receipt.
  • Taxes, buy-side — the purchase taxes template computing input VAT (the claimable half of the 21st — Procurement 1, Chapter 7), plus any charges rows. The template travels to the purchase invoice exactly as selling's travelled — and so do its errors, which is why the Draft check matters here too.
  • Terms and conditions — payment terms inherited from the master (the credit they extend you), delivery terms, and the T&C the commitment rides under.
  • Source links — the Material Request and/or Supplier Quotation this PO descends from: the chain of custody fields. A PO that names its ancestry can be audited in one minute; one that cannot is Chapter 9's business.

Draft, the six-box check, submit. Right supplier? rates as agreed or as quoted? dates realistic against lead times? target warehouses sane? tax template correct? terms intact? Thirty seconds, because submission — Chapter 3 — starts machinery that the whole company trades against. The PO that goes out wrong comes back as a receipt dispute, an invoice mismatch, or a warehouse surprise; the Draft check is the cheapest of the three conversations.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Creation discipline: where POs come from
lessons.html:
How a PO is born decides whether the commitment matches the need, the sourcing, and the agreed rates — or merely resembles them. Three legitimate births, one spine.

From the Material Request. The routine route: demand assembled in the queue (Procurement 3), the PO created FROM the request — items, quantities, target warehouses carrying over; the supplier and rate arriving from the masters (supplier-scoped Item Prices doing their quiet work); the request's ordered-percentage advancing. Consolidation lives here: multiple requests' rows drawn into one PO at pallet economics, each request tracking its own fulfilment — the buying-power thesis, executed document by document.

From the winning Supplier Quotation. The sourcing route (Procurement 4): the PO created FROM the awarded quotation, rates and terms exactly as quoted and negotiated, the chain request → RFQ → quotation → PO complete. This path's integrity IS the sourcing process's integrity: what was competed is what is committed, to the kobo.

Direct entry — the honest minority. Purchases without requests or sourcing exist legitimately per the firm's policy (Procurement 3's proportionality: the categories the policy exempted; genuine emergencies logged as exceptions). Direct entry fills the grid by hand, rates still fetching from the buying list — and the tell of a process problem is not direct entry existing but direct entry DOMINATING where policy requires the layers: if most POs have no demand or sourcing ancestry in a firm whose policy says they should, the governance above them is being bypassed, and the exceptions log (Procurement 4, Chapter 7) is where that becomes visible instead of normal.

The spine, stated once more. Documents made FROM their parents count against them; documents typed from scratch orphan the record — the fourth module in this track to say so, because procurement's chain is longer than selling's and every joint obeys the same law. The practical payoffs at this joint: zero transcription drift between quoted and committed; requests that close themselves; and the audit trail that answers WHO NEEDED THIS and HOW WAS THE SUPPLIER CHOSEN from the PO's own face.

One commitment, one PO. Resist fragmentation (three small POs to one supplier in one week because three requests arrived separately — the consolidation scan exists to prevent exactly this) and agglomeration (appending new needs onto an old open PO — new commitments get new documents; old paper does not house new deals). The PO maps one commercial commitment, and its identity is what receiving, invoicing, and every status hangs from.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — What submission changes: the incoming pipeline & the fulfilment ledger
lessons.html:
Submitting a Purchase Order changes the state of the business twice — and you already know both machines, because Selling 4 taught their mirror images.

Machine one: the incoming pipeline. The ordered quantities appear as incoming (expected) against each row's target warehouse. Nothing has arrived — arrival is the Purchase Receipt's act (Procurement 6) — but the expectation is now system state, and it completes the arithmetic you have met twice already: projected stock = actual − reserved + incoming. Selling 4 taught the reserved term; THIS document supplies the incoming term. The consequences ripple everywhere: reorder triggers see coverage on the way and stop re-requesting (Procurement 3's auto-replenishment reads this number — a submitted PO is what silences the trigger); sales sees sellable-soon; planning sees the pipeline by date. Which is also why stale open POs are poison in the exact inverse way stale sales orders were: a dead PO nobody closed keeps promising incoming forever — projected stock reads healthy, triggers stay silent, and the firm quietly runs out of what the system swears is on the way. Chapter 5's sweep exists for this; Chapter 9 meets it in the wild as the phantom-incoming disease.

Machine two: the fulfilment ledger. From submission the PO tracks per row: quantity ordered, received so far, billed so far — quantities and percentages. Every Purchase Receipt and every Purchase Invoice created FROM the order counts these down; the PO always knows what remains owed to you and what remains uninvoiced by the supplier. The from-scratch conviction lands harder on the buy side: a receipt typed loose moves real stock while the PO still shows goods owed — and the supplier's invoice, when it arrives, has nothing to match against, which is how the three-way match (Procurement 7's control) is quietly disarmed months before anyone needs it.

What the ledger feeds. The received/billed percentages drive the status word (Chapter 4); remaining quantities pre-fill the next receipt and the invoice match (exact remainders, never guesses); and across all POs, the purchase-order analysis reading is the firm's inbound backlog — what stands committed and unperformed, by supplier, by date, by naira.

What submission does NOT do. No stock moves, no expense books, no money is owed yet — receipt and invoice have their own moments (the timeline law's buy-side reading: order commits, receipt takes possession, invoice books the liability, payment settles it). A colleague asking why the bin has not changed after the PO went out gets that sentence, and the module it previews.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — The status language & the PO list as worklists
lessons.html:
A PO's status is computed arithmetic on the fulfilment ledger — never set by hand — and the list, filtered by it, becomes three different teams' worklists.

  • To Receive and Bill — freshly committed: goods not arrived, invoice not booked. Every PO starts here.
  • To Bill — received, not yet invoiced by the supplier (or their invoice not yet booked): possession taken, liability pending. This list is the match queue — Procurement 7's three-way match works it — and its age is worth watching from BOTH directions: your unbooked liabilities understate what you owe, and a supplier whose invoices chronically lag is a reconciliation risk compounding monthly (Procurement 1, Chapter 5's statement discipline catches the drift).
  • To Receive — invoiced ahead of arrival: the advance-billing and payment-before-shipment flows (the import deposit against documents). Money committed or booked; goods still owed — the status keeps the physical promise visible after finance has moved, exactly as Selling 4's To-Deliver did with the roles reversed.
  • Completed — both counts done; the PO retires from every pending list.

The worklists, by team. Receiving's week: To-Receive(-and-Bill) rows grouped by expected date — the inbound dock plan, staffed and scheduled from the system instead of from surprise trucks (Chapter 7's date honesty is what makes this view trustworthy). Finance's match queue: To Bill, oldest first, each receipt awaiting its invoice. Procurement's chase list: rows past their expected dates — the expediting queue, Chapter 7's craft. One list, three filters, three teams working from the same truth.

The per-supplier view. One supplier's open POs, all statuses, expected-date column visible: the screen to have open when that supplier calls, and the screen to open BEFORE calling them — what have we committed, what has arrived, what is late, what is unbilled, in one look. For your key manufacturers this view plus the payables view (Procurement 1) is the whole relationship on two tabs, the buy-side twin of the account screens Selling 4 and 7 built.

Status vs docstatus, once more. The fulfilment status (this chapter) is distinct from the document lifecycle (Draft / Submitted / Cancelled — Chapter 6's axis). Support conversations name which axis is in question: the commitment stands; the fulfilment is what moved — the same sentence as selling, the same clarity it buys.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Hold & Close: the two manual controls, inbound
lessons.html:
The ledger runs itself; two decisions stay human — and both matter MORE on the buy side, because their neglect distorts the number the whole company plans by.

Hold — the pause. A quality question surfaces mid-order (the batch documentation query on pharma lines), the supplier's compliance lapses, your own storage or cash needs a beat: Hold freezes the PO — commitment intact, incoming intact, fulfilment not actionable until released. The discipline transfers verbatim from Selling 4: a held PO carries a reason, an owner, and a dated next step, because an unowned hold is either forgotten (goods arrive into an unresolved question) or eternal (a live supply line strangled by a dead flag). Note the interplay with the supplier-level hold (Procurement 1, Chapter 6): the supplier hold blocks NEW documents by type; the PO hold pauses ONE commitment — different instruments, different scopes, chosen deliberately.

Close — the honest early ending. The canonical inbound case: the supplier delivered 260 of 300 and cannot supply the remainder — allocation shortage, discontinuation, or their own failure. Close ends the PO deliberately: the received 260 stand in history exactly as they happened; the undelivered 40's incoming expectation is released — projected stock stops counting phantom coverage, and (the step selling never needed) the reorder trigger can see the gap again: the shortfall re-enters the demand machinery to be resourced, typically to the second source at their scoped rate (the concentration remedy of Procurement 4, now operational). The rejected alternatives carry the same convictions as selling's: cancelling falsifies history (260 DID arrive); deleting rows mutilates a submitted document; receiving 40 to nowhere invents stock to satisfy a status.

The monthly sweep — the phantom-incoming vaccine. Selling 4's sweep chased ghost reservations that HID sellable stock; the inbound sweep chases the inverse and nastier disease: stale open POs whose phantom incoming INFLATES projected stock — triggers stay silent, replenishment never fires, and the firm stocks out with a system that swears goods are on the way. The ritual: open POs past their expected dates with no movement in N weeks — each one chased (Chapter 7's expediting), held with an owner, or closed honestly with its remainder released back into the demand machinery. On the sell side the ghost cost you stock you could not sell; on the buy side it costs you stock you never bought — and only one of those is discovered by a customer.

Reopening. A closed PO reopens only when the SAME commitment genuinely revives (the supplier's allocation returns for the same order at the same terms); new supply at new terms is a new PO. Old paper does not house new deals — fourth appearance, same law.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Amendments, cancellation & sourcing integrity
lessons.html:
Submitted POs are immutable; change walks through the formal doorway — and on the buy side, one amendment type carries a special warning.

Cancel, then Amend. Quantities change, a line is added, a date is renegotiated: cancel, amend, and the revision carries the same identity with its suffix (PO-00318-1), the original preserved, the chain readable — the machinery you know. Cancellation releases the incoming expectation (the pipeline un-promises; triggers may fire — correctly, since the goods are no longer coming) and re-opens the source request's claim where one exists, worth tidying deliberately.

The linked-documents constraint. A PO with submitted Purchase Receipts or Purchase Invoices against it will not simply cancel — the system refuses, because unwinding a commitment that partly HAPPENED would orphan real stock movements and real ledger entries. The lawful sequence is the one you learned outbound: unwind the children before the parent — cancel unexecuted drafts; route executed reality through purchase returns (Procurement 6) and debit notes (Procurement 7); then the PO cancels cleanly. The ticket to refuse is the same ticket: administrative force-deletion, which orphans ledgers and teaches the firm its documents are negotiable.

Rate amendments — the sourcing-integrity warning. Here the buy side carries a hazard selling did not: the temptation to amend a PO's RATE to match whatever the supplier's invoice eventually says. Understand precisely what that amendment does: the PO's rate is the COMMITTED price — the agreed Item Price or the competed quotation figure — and it is the standard the three-way match (Procurement 7) will hold the invoice against. Amend the rate to match the invoice and the match is satisfied by construction: the control is disarmed, the overcharge is laundered into agreement, and the sourcing chain's final link is quietly cut. The honest paths when a price genuinely changed: a documented renegotiation BEFORE amendment (the new rate agreed, noted, and encoded to the buying list so the change is policy, not drift), or the invoice DISPUTED against the standing committed rate (the match doing its job). What never happens: the standard bending to meet the deviation. This is the buy-side edition of the edited-invoice conviction from Selling 7, and it escalates the same way — as governance, not support.

Amend vs Close, the instrument choice. Corrections amend (the commitment was recorded wrong — wrong quantity agreed, missing line, wrong rate keyed against the quote). Endings close (the commitment was right; the supplier delivered what they will deliver). Amending a 300 down to 260 because the supplier stopped rewrites the promise to match the outcome; Close preserves that 300 was committed and 260 arrived — the truth the next negotiation with that supplier deserves to read.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The supplier's promise: acknowledgment, dates & expediting
lessons.html:
A PO sent is not a PO agreed. This chapter is the craft of turning your commitment into the supplier's promise — and managing that promise until the truck arrives.

Acknowledgment — the handshake. Every consequential PO gets a supplier acknowledgment: confirmation received, quantities and rates accepted, delivery date committed. Without it you hold a promise nobody made — the PO that emailed into a dead inbox (Procurement 1's primary-flag hygiene, at stakes), the order the supplier is silently unable to fill, the rate they will dispute at invoice time. The discipline is light: acknowledgment requested in the send, chased within days for open sends, and the supplier's committed date recorded — which may differ from your asked date, and the difference is a conversation NOW, not a surprise at required-by. An 11-person firm does this with a checklist column; a larger one with workflow — either way, unacknowledged POs are a standing short list someone owns.

Expected-date honesty. The row's expected dates are what receiving plans by and what the sweep (Chapter 5) and the chase (below) trigger from — so they are maintained as TRUTH: updated when the supplier's committed date differs from the ask, updated when a delay is notified, never edited to hide lateness (the mirror of Selling 4's plan-vs-mirror conviction: a schedule that only ever shows achievable dates because misses are edited away is not a schedule). Lateness recorded honestly is what makes the supplier measurable — the point of the last section.

Expediting — the chase craft. The chase list: rows past expected date (or approaching it on critical lines), worked oldest-and-most-critical first, with the same four-gear spirit as collections (Selling 7) pointed inbound: the pre-due confirmation on critical lines (still on for Tuesday? — cheap, and it surfaces slips early), the polite chase at slip with a new committed date extracted and RECORDED, escalation through the relationship for chronic lines, and the commercial gears where they exist (the second source warmed up; the shortfall short-closed and resourced — Chapter 5's machinery). Expediting is a system, not a mood: predictable, polite, relentless — the three adjectives again, buying instead of collecting.

Measuring the promise: OTIF-to-commitment. With honest dates and recorded slips, each supplier's on-time-in-full performance against their OWN committed dates becomes computable — the single most useful supplier metric there is, and the primary feed of the scorecard Procurement 8 builds. The craft points: measure against the supplier's commitment (not your original wish — that measures your optimism), measure in-full separately from on-time (the chronic 90%-shipper is a different problem from the chronic late-shipper), and let the number do the relationship talking: the quarterly review that opens with your OTIF was 96%, thank you or 83%, let us talk about why is a review conducted from records — which, by now, you will recognise as this entire track's method.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: HealthTrade's POs in motion
lessons.html:
Two commitments from earlier modules now live their full lives. Every step names its chapter.

Thread one — the 300-carton Emzor PO (from Procurement 3's consolidation).

Step 1 — birth and handshake (Ch. 2, 7). Created from the three requests (auto 260, Ibadan gap 15, Abeokuta 25), rate fetching Emzor's scoped ₦9,600, target warehouse Central, VAT template computing input VAT. Acknowledgment requested in the send; Emzor confirms in two days — but commits 300 in TWO drops: 180 next week, 120 the week after. The row dates are updated to the committed schedule (Ch. 7's honesty): receiving now plans two dock days, and nobody is surprised by a half truck.

Step 2 — submission's machines (Ch. 3). Incoming 300 cartons (3,600 units) against Central: PARA-500's reorder trigger goes quiet — correctly, coverage is on the way; projected stock tells sales the truth.

Step 3 — the hold episode (Ch. 5). Before drop one, a NAFDAC batch-documentation query surfaces on one Emzor batch in the market. The PO goes on Hold — owner: procurement lead; next step: Emzor's QA letter by Friday — while the supplier-level record stays clean (one commitment paused, not the relationship blocked: the two instruments distinguished). The letter lands Thursday; hold released; drop one arrives on its committed date.

Step 4 — the short-close and the resource (Ch. 5). Drop one delivers 180; drop two arrives at 80 — Emzor's allocation is short and the final 40 cannot come this cycle. The PO is Closed at 260 received: the 40's incoming releases, projected stock tells the truth, the trigger sees the gap — and the demand machinery resources it: a PO to the backup distributor at THEIR scoped ₦9,850 (Procurement 2's second atom, and Procurement 4's concentration logic, both earning their keep). History reads truthfully: 300 committed, 260 delivered, gap resourced in four days. That sentence will open the next Emzor review.

Thread two — the chiller PO (from Procurement 4's award).

Step 5 — the chain complete (Ch. 2). PO from Vendor A's revised quotation: ₦1.395m, Net-15, exactly as awarded — request → RFQ → quotes → comparison → PO, auditable from the document's own face.

Step 6 — expediting a critical line (Ch. 7). Two-week lead against a six-week launch: comfortable — so the craft is the pre-due confirmation, not the panic chase. Day 10's still on for Thursday? surfaces a two-day slip (a compressor delivery on their side); the new committed date is recorded, receiving replans, the launch holds with slack to spare. The slip enters Vendor A's OTIF record — 96% and honest, which their quarterly review will open by acknowledging.

Month-end reads (Ch. 4, 7). The PO list by status: nothing stale (the sweep found only the closed Emzor remainder, already resourced); the match queue holds two receipts awaiting invoices (Procurement 7 inherits them); OTIF per supplier updates from committed dates. The inbound side now runs the way the outbound side learned to: on documents, on arithmetic, on promises with owners.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & support patterns
lessons.html:
The commitment layer's scar tissue — and on the buy side, the most expensive diseases are the QUIET ones, because they distort the number everything plans by. Symptom → disease → fix.

Pattern 1 — "We stocked out while the system showed healthy projected stock." Disease: phantom incoming — stale open POs promising goods forever (Ch. 3, 5). The trigger stayed silent because coverage was on the way; the way had ended months ago. Fix: the monthly sweep — chase, hold with owner, or close with the remainder released into the demand machinery; the inverse ghost of Selling 4's, and the one a customer discovers first.

Pattern 2 — "Goods arrived; the PO says they are still owed; the invoice matches nothing." Disease: the from-scratch Purchase Receipt (Ch. 3) — stock moved, ledger orphaned, three-way match disarmed in advance. Fix: reconcile the orphan against the PO deliberately; retrain the create-from reflex — fourth module, same spine.

Pattern 3 — "The PO rate was amended to match the invoice." Disease: the sourcing-integrity breach (Ch. 6) — the match satisfied by construction, the overcharge laundered, the competed rate's final link cut. Fix: revert; dispute the invoice against the standing rate or paper the renegotiation properly and encode it; close the permission that allowed it — governance, not support.

Pattern 4 — "The supplier never saw the order." Disease: no acknowledgment discipline (Ch. 7) riding on a dead primary contact (Procurement 1's Pattern 1, compounding). The promise existed only on your side. Fix: acknowledgment requested and chased as routine; the unacknowledged-PO list owned; the contact hygiene repaired at the master.

Pattern 5 — "Receiving found out about the truck when it arrived." Disease: expected dates unmaintained (Ch. 7) — asked dates never replaced by committed dates, slips never recorded, the dock planning blind. Fix: date honesty as routine — committed dates recorded at acknowledgment, updated at every notified slip — and the receiving week read from the To-Receive view it can finally trust.

Pattern 6 — "Two POs to the same supplier for the same demand." Disease: duplicate commitment — two buyers, or the request ordered twice because tracking was orphaned (Ch. 2; Procurement 3's Pattern 6, matured into money). Fix: consolidate — close or cancel the junior twin after moving real fulfilment references; the consolidation scan and the open-PO check before creating, taught as reflex.

Pattern 7 — "The supplier stopped at 260, so we amended the PO to 260." Disease: amend-close confusion (Ch. 6) — history rewritten to match the outcome, and the next negotiation robbed of the truthful sentence you committed 300 and delivered 260. Fix: Close, with the remainder released and resourced; corrections amend, endings close — the distinction, verbatim from Selling 4, because it is the same machine.

The law. Procurement 1: purchase documents are downstream of supplier masters. Procurement 2: cost truth begins at the item. Procurement 3: the request layer separates need from commitment. Procurement 4: sourcing is a decision record, not a lunch. This module adds the fifth: the Purchase Order is the single source of inbound truth — every receipt and invoice is made FROM it, every status is arithmetic ON it, the incoming pipeline the whole firm plans by is promised BY it, and the supplier's measurable promise hangs from its honest dates. Protect that role, sweep its ghosts, and never bend its rates to meet an invoice — and the receiving dock, the match queue, and the reorder triggers all inherit a truth they can execute without a phone call.
